articles.title: More than 1,000 hidden coral reefs have been mapped across northern Australia after scientists combined hundreds of satellite images
articles.summary: Thousands of kilometres of northern Australia's coastline can look deceptively simple from above.
articles.body: Thousands of kilometres of northern Australia's coastline can look deceptively simple from above. Much of the water is clouded by sediment, making coral formations difficult to distinguish from the shifting patterns on the surface. According to the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS), in 2026, scientists found a way to make those hidden structures easier to see without sending a survey vessel into the water. By combining large numbers of satellite images, researchers from the Australian Institute of Marine Science and the University of Queensland identified and mapped more than 1,000 coral reefs that had not previously appeared on detailed maps. The work stretches from Western Australia towards western Cape York in Queensland, giving marine planners a much clearer picture of reefs that had remained largely unmapped.How one researcher turned changing satellite images into a reef-mapping toolAs reported by AIMS , the idea behind the project began years before the new maps were produced. Dr Eric Lawrey, an e-Atlas project manager at the Australian Institute of Marine Science, had been looking at satellite imagery of Australia's northern coastline when he started noticing shapes that appeared to be reefs. There was a problem, though. A single image rarely gave a reliable view.Northern Australian waters can be heavily affected by suspended sediment, leaving the sea looking almost uniformly coloured from above. Reefs beneath the surface were difficult to separate from the constantly moving patterns created by the water. Lawrey realised that the movement itself could help solve the problem.Hundreds of images revealed what one could hideRather than relying on an individual satellite photograph, the team combined roughly 200 images of the same areas, taken at different times. The changing water patterns moved from image to image. The reefs did not. When the images were combined, those shifting surface effects became less prominent while the persistent shapes of reefs were strengthened. Structures that had been difficult to distinguish in individual photographs became much easier to recognise.It was a form of desktop exploration. There was no need for the researchers to travel by boat simply to establish where many of these formations were located. Once the reefs could be seen more clearly, their boundaries could be mapped.More than 1,000 reefs emerged from the imageryAccording to AIMS official X (Twitter) post, the mapping revealed more than 1,000 previously uncharted coral reefs across northern Australia.The source describes the area as extending from the Houtman Abrolhos in Western Australia to western Cape York in Queensland. Many of the reefs are considerably smaller than those associated with the Great Barrier Reef, but their combined presence changed the picture of how extensively coral habitat is distributed along the northern coastline.The team ultimately produced a much broader classification of the region, identifying more than 3,600 coral reefs alongside about 2,900 rocky reefs.Why mapping the newly visible reefs was harder than expectedThe technology made the reefs visible, but it did not turn the entire process into an automatic exercise. Early attempts to use automated methods produced too many false positives. The team therefore relied heavily on manual interpretation.Reportedly, it took around 700 hours to digitise the reefs and assign classifications to them. That work also required different approaches in different parts of the coastline. The formations were not all shaped in the same way, and local geology and tidal conditions affected what appeared in the imagery. The Kimberley was particularly demanding. Tidal ranges there can reach about 12 metres, producing reef structures that look very different from those found elsewhere.Some reefs had unusual structuresThe mapping exercise was not simply a matter of finding patches of coral and drawing lines around them. Some reefs occur high in the intertidal zone, with algal ridges surrounding them. Others form structures with shallow lagoons and walls that allow coral to grow vertically. The team also encountered ancient shoreline rocky reefs, fringing coral reefs, oceanic banks and sand banks while building a more detailed picture of the northern Australian seascape. This variation meant the researchers had to understand the physical character of each region before deciding how best to interpret the satellite imagery.Northern Australia had been poorly mappedMarine charts had provided some information before this project, but they were designed primarily for navigation. Their purpose was to alert vessels to hazards rather than produce a detailed ecological inventory. Coral reefs and rocky reefs were not necessarily separated in the way a marine habitat map would require. As a result, large sections of the northern coastline had remained comparatively poorly surveyed from an ecological mapping perspective.The maps could change how marine areas are managedKnowing where habitats are located matters for the people responsible for managing coastal waters. The new datasets give marine planners, Traditional Owners and other managers more detailed information about the distribution of reefs. That can be particularly useful in areas where previous mapping provided only a broad indication of underwater hazards or habitat.The researchers applied the imagery approach to the Great Barrier Reef, where it was used alongside a separate University of Queensland effort to remap outer reefs. That work identified hundreds of additional reefs and helped remove formations that had previously been incorrectly identified as reefs. The revised Great Barrier Reef dataset was under review by the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority at the time of the AIMS announcement, as reported by AIMS official website.You use AI every day. articles.title: 5 held in UK for suspected plot to attack air base used by US
articles.summary: LONDON: Five men were arrested by police early Sunday morning in a tiny village in UK’s Gloucestershire on suspicion of preparing terrorist attacks at a
articles.body: LONDON: Five men were arrested by police early Sunday morning in a tiny village in UK’s Gloucestershire on suspicion of preparing terrorist attacks at a military base used by the US Air Force.At 12.45am local time, Gloucestershire police received a call from a resident of Whelford, relating to three suspicious white vans travelling towards RAF Fairford.Whelford is a one-minute car drive from the military base which is heavily populated by the US Air Force and has been used by the US to launch its bombers against Iran since March.Armed officers responded and arrested five men on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act. They were then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.On Sunday night, they remained in custody and counter-terrorism police are leading the investigation.Photos showed the suspects lying in the road shirtless and handcuffed surrounded by armed officers. Their nationalities are not yet known.Footage showed army bomb disposal robots examining the three white vans on Sunday afternoon.About 85 households in Whelford were woken up by police early Sunday and forced to evacuate their homes owing to fears the vans contained explosive materials. Many are now staying in a local leisure centre with their pets.Locals said tractors, JCBs and concrete walls had been put in front of the military base gates.A spokesperson for the US Air Force said its personnel based at RAF Fairford “remain vigilant”. “We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families.”US president Donald Trump described the arrests as “fantastic”. “They were looking to do big damage. We had them under review for a long time and we got them,” he told reporters in Illinois.Iran’s Revolutionary Guards had warned in July that any UK base used in strikes against Iran would be a legitimate target.Authorities have not ruled out an Islamist plot or Russian involvement.You use AI every day. articles.title: Rhode Island federal judge orders revival of $7 billion Solar for All program canceled by Trump administration’s EPA in August 2025, rules agency overstepped its authority
articles.summary: More than a year after federal regulators canceled a $7 billion solar energy grant program, a Rhode Island federal judge has ordered the government to
articles.body: More than a year after federal regulators canceled a $7 billion solar energy grant program, a Rhode Island federal judge has ordered the government to revive the initiative, ruling that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency overstepped its statutory authority when it terminated the program.The ruling, issued by U.S. District Judge Mary S. McElroy of the U.S. District Court for Rhode Island, comes in a lawsuit filed by union laborers, solar installation companies, a homeowner and nonprofit advocates who challenged the EPA’s August 2025 decision to terminate the Solar for All program, as reported by Rhode Island Current.However, the ruling does not immediately mean the money will begin flowing again. The EPA said it is reviewing the decision and considering its options for appeal, while attorneys for the plaintiffs say they do not yet know how the administration will respond.$49.3 million was allocated to Rhode IslandSolar for All was created under the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act to expand access to solar power among low- and moderate-income households and disadvantaged communities.The EPA awarded and obligated the full $7 billion in grants in 2024 to states, local governments, nonprofits and tribal organizations. Rhode Island was allocated approximately $49.3 million through the state Office of Energy Resources.Rhode Island had already begun preparing to administer its grant before the funding was terminated. The state had spent about $89,000 on administrative preparation when the money was clawed back, according to state officials cited in the lawsuit coverage.Nationwide, the five-year program had been projected by the Biden administration to help approximately 900,000 households save $350 million annually on energy bills and create about 200,000 jobs.EPA cited new federal legislationThe Trump administration’s EPA ended Solar for All in August 2025, several months after President Donald Trump took office.Federal regulators argued that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law on July 4, 2025, had rescinded congressional authority for the program and allowed the government to claw back unspent funds.Judge McElroy rejected that interpretation. In her ruling, she determined that funds already obligated under the program were not automatically transformed into unrestricted money simply because Congress repealed the statutory provision underlying the program.Plaintiffs say the program could still create jobsThe Rhode Island AFL-CIO was among the plaintiffs challenging the cancellation. Its president, Patrick Crowley, said the program could significantly expand solar deployment in the state while creating work for electricians, ironworkers and other skilled tradespeople.“We already have trained tradespeople to start doing this work,” Crowley said, according to Rhode Island Current.The program’s cancellation had also disrupted preparations by nonprofits and businesses involved in solar installation, financing and education.Kevin Hubbard, executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Rhode Island and an attorney representing the plaintiffs, said the ruling leaves uncertainty over what happens next.“The result is maddeningly difficult to talk about what happens next because we just don’t know what they’ll do,” Hubbard said.Rhode Island cannot yet move ahead with its grantAlthough McElroy rejected the cancellation, she did not specify exactly how federal administrators must restart Solar for All.One possibility would be allowing existing grant recipients to continue with the awards they had already received. Another could involve requiring recipients to reapply for the competitive funding, potentially causing additional delays.Rhode Island officials are also waiting for clarity before moving forward with the state’s $49.3 million allocation.Robert Beadle, a spokesperson for the Rhode Island Office of Energy Resources, said the state needs to know the outcome of the legal challenge before proceeding with the grant.Solar for All was intended to expand access to clean energyThe legal battle centers on a program designed to make residential solar more accessible to households that might otherwise struggle to afford installation.The original program was part of the federal government's broader effort under the Inflation Reduction Act to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions while expanding clean-energy access in low-income and disadvantaged communities.Jennifer L. Wood, executive director of the Rhode Island Center for Justice, another plaintiff, said the ruling could help restore an avenue for lower-income Rhode Islanders facing high housing and utility costs.The Southern Environmental Law Center, Lawyers for Good Government and the Conservation Law Foundation also represented the plaintiffs.For now, the future of the $7 billion Solar for All program remains tied to the federal government's next legal move. The EPA is reviewing Judge McElroy's ruling, meaning the dispute could continue through an appeal before the funding is fully restored or projects resume.You use AI every day. articles.title: A $45 million San Francisco mansion once owned by Larry Ellison kept its new buyer secret for a year; the 11,000-square-foot Billionaires Row property has now been traced to investor Chuck Esserman
articles.summary: The mystery buyer behind one of San Francisco’s most secretive real estate deals has finally been identified, nearly a year after an off-market sale
articles.body: The mystery buyer behind one of San Francisco’s most secretive real estate deals has finally been identified, nearly a year after an off-market sale transferred a $45 million mansion on Billionaires Row. Private equity investor Chuck Esserman bought the 10,742-square-foot Pacific Heights home formerly owned by Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, according to the San Francisco Standard. The off-market deal closed in December 2025 under a trust tied to Esserman, ending months of speculation among local luxury real estate brokers about who had bought the property. Esserman is the co-founder and CEO of San Francisco-based private equity firm TSG Consumer Partners. He bought the estate without a public listing. The purchase adds to a string of expensive real estate deals linked to Esserman. In 2023, an LLC connected to him and his wife, Ivette, bought singer Celine Dion’s Las Vegas mansion for $30 million.Decades of growth on Billionaires RowThe property at 2850 Broadway has risen sharply in value since Ellison bought it 37 years ago. The Oracle co-founder purchased the home in 1988 for $3.9 million and later sold it off-market for $45 million. The December 2025 transaction was San Francisco’s biggest home sale of the year. The home was designed by architect William Wurster in 1958. It was later extensively renovated for Ellison by designer Olle Lundberg. The changes left little of Wurster’s original design and gave the house a style influenced by Japanese gardens, with courtyards, gardens and views toward the waterfront. Despite the home’s $45 million sale price, its tax assessment was far lower. Public records show the property had an assessed value of about $8.9 million in 2025. California’s Proposition 13 limits increases in a property’s assessed value after a sale, helping explain why long-time owners can have assessments well below current market values. The 2850 Broadway estate sits on a prominent corner near the Lyon Street Steps on the western side of Pacific Heights. The five-bedroom, six-bathroom home covers 10,742 square feet. It features large living and entertainment areas, extensive windows and views toward the Golden Gate Bridge, Alcatraz and San Francisco Bay.High-profile neighbours in Pacific HeightsThe purchase puts Esserman among some of the wealthiest people living along the same stretch of Broadway. Next door at 2840 Broadway is the home of Laurene Powell Jobs, founder of the Emerson Collective and widow of Apple co-founder Steve Jobs. Powell Jobs bought the neighboring property for about $71 million in 2024, setting San Francisco’s record for the most expensive home sale. The stretch of Pacific Heights often called Billionaires Row is also home to former Apple chief design officer Jony Ive, Yelp CEO Jeremy Stoppelman, Zynga founder Mark Pincus and venture capitalist Peter Thiel. The San Francisco Standard reported that the mystery surrounding Ellison’s sale led to speculation about possible buyers, including Elon Musk and Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi. The Standard later confirmed that the buyer was a trust tied to Esserman. Esserman and his family have previously used private entities for high-value home purchases. In addition to the $30 million Celine Dion property in Las Vegas, an LLC connected to Esserman and his wife bought Peter Thiel’s former San Francisco home for $7.4 million in 2018. Esserman’s purchase also comes as San Francisco’s luxury housing market continues to see major sales. Powell Jobs’ $71 million purchase remains the city’s residential sales record, while Ellison’s $45 million deal was the largest San Francisco home sale of 2025. Neither Esserman nor representatives of TSG Consumer Partners publicly commented on the purchase or explained what he plans to do with the property.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Fetterman claims Democratic ‘big tent’ has more room for ‘America deserved 9/11’ than Israel support
articles.summary: John Fetterman says the Democratic Party's big tent now welcomes those who say America "deserved 9/11" more than pro-Israel Democrats like him.
articles.body: Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., claimed on Saturday that the Democratic Party’s "big tent" had become more accommodating of people who say America "deserved 9/11" than Democrats who strongly support Israel, as the Pennsylvania senator explained why the issue has increasingly put him at odds with parts of his party. Fetterman made the comparison at the Texas Tribune Festival in Austin while CBS News chief Washington correspondent Major Garrett asked whether there were any circumstances under which he would leave the Democratic Party. "It’s easier to be included in that big tent to say ‘America deserved 9/11’ or America is ‘worse than Al-Qaeda’ than being very proud to stand on the side of Israel," Fetterman said. "More and more members of my caucus are becoming more and more anti-Israel." SEN JOHN FETTERMAN PLEDGES TO BE 'LAST MAN STANDING' IN THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IN SUPPORT OF ISRAEL Fetterman saying America "deserved 9/11" was a reference to streamer Hasan Piker, who made the remark during a 2019 livestream before later saying he "obviously" did not believe Americans deserved the terrorist attacks. Fetterman pointed to the interest in Piker's appearances as evidence of where he believed political enthusiasm was building on the left. "I’m just describing that’s where a lot of the energy on the left is in my party," Fetterman said. The tension comes as Democratic voters’ attitudes toward Israel have shifted sharply. A Pew Research Center survey conducted in March found 80% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents held an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 53% in 2022. Overall, 60% of American adults viewed Israel unfavorably. HASAN PIKER IS BECOMING THE 'FACE OF THE PROGRESSIVE MOVEMENT,' FORMER DEMOCRATIC OPERATIVE WARNS "80% Democrats have a negative view on Israel," Fetterman said. "If America stops supporting Israel or turns their back on Israel, that must mean that we don't even believe in ourselves anymore. I mean that's that's our special ally and that is the kinds of values and the kinds of the you know how we live here that's that only exists in one place in that region and that's that's Israel." "If our party ever becomes, and just makes it official, the anti-Israel party, that’s when I would leave, because that’s been a moral clarity for me," Fetterman said. Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin addressed that tension in comments to Fox News Digital on Monday, defending Democrats as a "big tent" party while distancing the DNC from Piker. DEMOCRATS CONDEMNING HASAN PIKER AS BACKLASH SPREADS THROUGH PARTY "Let me just say that I think it’s absolutely disgusting and deplorable the things that Hasan Piker has said," Martin said. "But he does not represent the Democratic Party, and he certainly doesn’t represent the viewpoints of almost every one of our candidates and our elected officials." Fox News Digital reached out to Piker for comment, but did not immediately receive a response. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fetterman also referenced resolutions introduced by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., while discussing Democratic opposition to Israeli military assistance. In April, 40 Senate Democrats voted to block a $295 million sale of bulldozers to Israel and 36 supported blocking a $151.8 million sale of 1,000-pound bombs. Those resolutions did not concern Iron Dome funding, which Fetterman separately cited Saturday as an example of defensive assistance to Israel.

articles.title: Bessent says Iran will have 'nothing left to trade' within two weeks as oil lifeline dries up
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Iran will complete its final oil shipments to China within two weeks, leaving Tehran with "nothing left to trade."
articles.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent predicted Sunday that Iran will complete its remaining oil shipments to China within two weeks, leaving Tehran with "nothing left to trade for anything" as the Trump administration intensifies its economic pressure campaign against the regime. Bessent said only about 15 million barrels of Iranian oil remain out for delivery now that the U.S. is blockading the ports, describing the dwindling shipments as evidence that Operation Economic Outcast has left Tehran economically isolated. "They will have nothing to trade for anything, probably within the next two weeks. They are going to make their final deliveries of oil to China, and then they will have nothing," he said. MILLIONS OF BARRELS OF IRANIAN OIL SIT BEYOND TRUMP BLOCKADE AS HE VOWS ‘ZERO LEAKAGE’ The Treasury chief said he believed Iran was "feeling the pressure," leading to their renewed interest in striking a deal. President Donald Trump rejected Tehran's latest proposal on Saturday, telling Axios on Sunday that "they overplayed their hand." "I expect more talks with Iran [this week]," Trump told the outlet during a phone interview. "They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make. It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand." IRAN ‘MISCALCULATING’ BY BETTING ON MIDTERMS AFTER 3-HOUR TALKS, TRUMP OFFICIALS WARN Tehran had offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a highly trafficked waterway in the region that is critical to global oil shipping. Bessent said it's already open. "We're averaging now 15 to 22 million barrels a day. It was at about 20 pre-conflict . . . So think of it this way, Larry," he said. "The score is the United States, one billion — more than one billion barrels have gotten out — Iran, zero." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The point of Operation Economic Outcast is to ensure that Iran adheres to the terms of a potential future deal, Bessent added. "They are isolated from the world. They're a pariah state. And my job is to make sure that, when they come with a deal, that they want to stick to it. They did not stick to the MOU [Memorandum of Understanding]. And, next time, if there is a deal — that's at President Trump's discretion — that they will stick to it, because they are on their knees." Fox News Digital's Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

articles.title: Meet Sister Stephanie Baliga: Once an aspiring elite runner, she became a nun and raised over $2.6 million through the Chicago Marathon; she’s still running to help families in need
articles.summary: Sister Stephanie Baliga once dreamed of becoming an elite athlete.
articles.body: Sister Stephanie Baliga once dreamed of becoming an elite athlete. Today, the former Division I runner is using that same passion for running to help feed families and senior citizens in her Chicago community.For the past 15 years, Baliga has taken part in the Chicago Marathon as part of the Mission of Our Lady of the Angels (MOLA) charity team. According to MOLA, the marathon team has raised more than $2.6 million between 2011 and 2025, helping support the organisation’s food pantry and community services.This fall, Baliga and nearly 200 members of Team OLA are expected to return for the 16th consecutive Chicago Marathon, with a fundraising goal of $500,000.Sister Stephanie’s journey from running to religious lifeBaliga began running when she was nine years old, and the sport quickly became central to her identity.“I started running when I was 9, and running became my life,” she told WTTW. “It was how I defined myself and who I was.”As a student-athlete at the University of Illinois, Baliga was the sixth-fastest freshman runner in the nation. She trained for hours each day and was preparing for a potential professional career.At the time, even a marathon time of 2 hours and 53 minutes, fast enough to qualify for the Boston Marathon, did not feel good enough to her.“The challenge of being an elite athlete is that you’re never satisfied with anything you’re doing,” she said.Her path changed when she fractured her foot during her sophomore year. Forced to spend less time running, she turned toward prayer and eventually realised she wanted to devote her life to God.“Jesus saw me for who I was. He was not looking for my straight A’s or my fast running times; he was just seeking to love me wherever I was at,” Baliga said.Her running now helps feed hundreds of familiesBaliga eventually found a way to combine her faith with her lifelong passion for running.Through the MOLA marathon team, she has spent the past 15 years raising money for the organisation’s food pantry, which serves hundreds of families every week.“We serve about 400 to 500 families in person every Tuesday and we send about 300 deliveries to senior citizens between Monday and Tuesday each week,” Baliga said. “It totally changed the way I live my life.”Father Bob Lombardo, who opened MOLA, said the organisation serves people regardless of their faith.“As we like to say, we do what we do because we’re Catholic, not because the people we serve are Catholic,” he told WTTW.Marathon fundraising helped sustain the pantryThe charity's marathon efforts have had a significant impact on the food pantry, particularly during a period when demand increased sharply.“The marathon funding was key to expanding the pantry in 2018, 2019 and 2020, and was very key to us sustaining an extremely large pantry during the pandemic,” Baliga said.The team raised about $20,000 during its first marathon. Over the years, that total grew to more than $2.6 million.Reflecting on the amount raised, Baliga said, “It was insane. You’re like, ‘Woah, look at all those zeros! That’s a lot of zeros.’ The Lord provides.”Team OLA prepares for another Chicago MarathonBaliga and nearly 200 Team OLA runners are preparing to run the Chicago Marathon for the 16th consecutive year.The team has set a goal of raising $500,000 this year. Baliga and the team also took part in a half marathon on June 10 as part of their preparations, raising around $16,000.The full marathon team had raised more than $184,000 toward this year’s goal, according to the information provided by MOLA.Supporters have also embraced the team’s mission. Other nuns and supporters have turned out with signs including “You vati-CAN do it” and “May God have mercy on your soles,” along with a cardboard cutout of Pope Leo.‘The Lord provides’MOLA describes Team OLA’s mission as raising awareness and funds for the organisation while offering the time, energy and physical discomfort involved in marathon training in support of the people it serves.For Baliga, the meaning of running has changed dramatically.What once represented a pursuit of faster times and athletic perfection is now a way to help put food on the tables of families and senior citizens.“You’re like, ‘Woah, look at all those zeros! That’s a lot of zeros,’” she said of the team’s fundraising achievement.“The Lord provides,” Baliga added. “God’s will is whatever is in front of you right now.”You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2013, Maryland restored Fishing Battery Island with sand and 60,000 plants, and much of its 12-acre habitat footprint remained 10 years later
articles.summary: In 2013, Maryland restored Fishing Battery Island in the northern Chesapeake Bay using sediment placed around the remains of the historic man-made island.
articles.body: In 2013, Maryland restored Fishing Battery Island in the northern Chesapeake Bay using sediment placed around the remains of the historic man-made island. The project, carried out by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, restored 12 acres of intertidal and upland habitat and included planting 60,000 native plants. The sediment was 95% medium-grained sand and was used to create a U-shaped berm designed to reach 7 feet above Mean Lower Low Water. Ten years later, much of the island’s designed footprint remained, with surviving switchgrass and trees that had naturally established across parts of the site.How was Fishing Battery Island restored with sedimentThe restoration involved placing sediment around the remains of Fishing Battery Island to form a tall U-shaped berm. According to a report by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the berm was designed to be 125 feet wide across the top and reach an elevation of 7 feet above Mean Lower Low Water. Its outer edge was graded to a 10:1 slope, while the inner edge was graded more steeply at 5:1 towards the existing island platform.The sediments used for the project were described as 95% medium-grained sand. The report states that there was no structural component to the built island, meaning there was no sediment containment feature or shoreline hardening. Sediment placement was completed in early spring 2013, after which the island was planted with native species suited to different elevation zones.Why were 1,600 more plants added later in 2013As part of the 2013 restoration, approximately 60,000 plants were planted across the island. The planting was intended to establish vegetation appropriate for the different elevation zones of the restored feature. Heavy human foot traffic and grazing by geese led to an additional planting effort later that year.In autumn 2013, a further 1,600 plants were planted, and 3 acres were seeded. The report states that this additional work was intended to protect the shoreline from erosion and impede foot traffic across the island. Apart from this additional planting, the site report records showed no formal maintenance of the project.How much of Fishing Battery Island remained after 10 yearsA comparison of the island's 2013 and 2023 extents showed that much of the designed footprint remained in place. According to the report, erosion affected the northern shoreline and the westernmost portions, particularly the outer tips of the U-shaped island. The island covered approximately 16 acres in 2014, while by 2015 its total area had declined to 10 acres and remained relatively stable thereafter.Elevation surveys conducted in 2023 showed that surveyed elevations along the island's higher central spine were approximately 50 centimetres (1.5 feet) lower than the designed elevations. The report states that the reason for this elevation loss was unclear, while noting that gradual slumping of the steep slopes, potentially exacerbated by human foot traffic, may have contributed. The central higher-elevation area remained above Mean High Water and was vegetated with switchgrass.How did switchgrass and trees grow on Fishing Battery IslandBy 2023, the planted switchgrass was described as successful and appeared to be thriving, although it had not formed a dense canopy. Planting rows were still visible in aerial imagery 10 years after construction. The report also records natural recruitment of tree species including locust, oak, sycamore and willow.The original restoration design included emergent grasses along the inner shoreline to establish a marsh fringe. By 2023, the report found no evidence of the planted marsh vegetation along that shoreline. Instead, much of the inner shoreline was densely vegetated with trees. The report concludes that, 10 years after construction, Fishing Battery Island continued to provide habitat and recreational benefits while protecting the remaining historic lighthouse from wave energy.You use AI every day. articles.body: IShowSpeed was once again impressed by Virat Kohli after the Indian cricket star scored his 55th ODI century against West Indies. articles.title: Supersonic Russian jets trigger joint scramble by NATO allies amid Putin 'clowns' jab
articles.summary: Finnish F/A-18 Hornets and Swedish Gripens scrambled jointly for the first time to intercept supersonic Russian military jets over the Gulf of Finland.
articles.body: Finnish and Swedish fighter jets scrambled for the first time on Sept. 24 to intercept supersonic Russian military aircraft flying over the Gulf of Finland, marking a major milestone in Nordic defense cooperation amid heightened tensions with Moscow. The mission also came one day before Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed European warnings about the threat from Moscow in the region and mocked Estonia's new defense minister over the Baltic state's preparations for a potential Russian attack. Finnish F/A-18 Hornets and Swedish JAS 39 Gripens were scrambled after Russian aircraft were detected in the international airspace, according to the Swedish Armed Forces. US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS The Russian formation included a Tu-134 transport plane, a high-altitude, supersonic MiG-31 interceptors designed to detect and engage long-range threats; and Su-30 multirole fighter jets which are designed for air-to-air and air-to-ground combat. "This is what close cooperation looks like in practice," Maj. Gen. Jonas Wikman, commander of the Swedish Air Force, said in a statement following the joint operation. "Built over years on trust and strong personal relationships, we can now operate seamlessly together — as air forces, as nations and as Allies." Concern over Russian military activity along NATO’s eastern flank has grown following a string of airspace violations. These include Russian drones entering Polish airspace, a Mi-8 helicopter crossing from Kaliningrad into Poland, drones crashing in Romania and Moldova, and armed Russian jets entering Estonian airspace before being intercepted by NATO aircraft on Sept. 18. BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT In Estonia, Defense Minister Martin Herem warned that Russia could be capable of using military force against Estonia within a year and argued that Tallinn must determine whether its defenses are sufficient for such a scenario. Prime Minister Kristen Michal stated that the government is ready to shut down border crossing points on short notice if threat assessments change, according to reports. Speaking at the St. Petersburg International United Cultures Forum on Friday, Putin pushed back against such warnings. "Many people in Europe say they expect an attack from Russia and therefore claim they must prepare for war with Russia," Putin said. "I want to emphasize once again: we are not preparing for military action against Europe. We have no such plans, no basis for them, and, most importantly, no real motive to escalate the situation with Europe." Putin then mocked Herem's warnings: "As we jokingly say in Russia: 'The circus has left, but the clowns remain.' It is political clowning. ... Clearly, these statements are complete nonsense and absurdity," Putin said, according to EurAsia Daily. FOREIGN LEADER ON PUTIN’S DOORSTEP SOUNDS ALARM OVER IRAN FUELING MOSCOW’S WAR MACHINE Estonia sits across the Gulf of Finland from Finland, with the three countries forming part of NATO's increasingly integrated northern and eastern defenses amid concerns about Russian military activity. Finland formally joined NATO as its 31st member in April 2023, roughly doubling the alliance's land border with Russia. Sweden followed as the 32nd member in March 2024. Estonia, which regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, has been a NATO member since 2004. The Baltic Sea region has also remained on heightened alert following incidents involving gas pipelines, sabotage and hybrid threats since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Reuters has reported. NATO said in June that it was enhancing protection of its eastern members in the cyber and space domains while helping countries build resilience against what it describes as hostile Russian actions, including cyberattacks, sabotage and airspace violations. NATO says its military activities along the eastern flank are entirely defensive and that it is "ready, willing and able to defend every Ally." FINLAND'S STUBB CREDITS TRUMP FOR PUSHING UKRAINE PEACE TALKS WHILE DISMISSING RUSSIAN INVASION FEARS The alliance has said an attack against any member would be met with a "resounding response." NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte recently underscored Washington's role in the alliance during a visit to Iowa, telling The Associated Press that Putin "knows that the United States and Europe are totally intertwined." "We have to make sure that we are prepared, we are strong, and he knows it," Rutte said. "And if he does anything silly, he knows our reaction will be tough," he warned. European intelligence officials said Sept. 24 that Russia could test NATO's defenses. Denmark's Defense Intelligence Service assessed the risk of a limited Russian military attack against a NATO country in the coming months as "low but growing" and said Moscow is expected to intensify its hybrid campaign against NATO and the West. articles.title: HM Amit Shah recalls Ashok Singhal's role in Ram temple movement
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Lauding former VHP leader Ashok Singhal as an inspiration and hero, home minister Amit Shah Sunday said Singhal believed that India could
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Lauding former VHP leader Ashok Singhal as an inspiration and hero, home minister Amit Shah Sunday said Singhal believed that India could attain a position of glory only by removing the "stigma of slavery" and constructing a grand Ram temple in its place in Ayodhya."The essence of his life, his penance, his simplicity and his dedication and endeavour are qualities worthy of emulation by every young person," Shah said at the inaugural ceremony of the centenary year celebrations to mark his birth anniversary. RSS general secretary Dattatreya Hosabole was among the Hindutva figures present at the event.It was only after PM Narendra Modi took office that govt obstacles were removed and a grand Ram temple was built, Shah said. He said the image of Singhal wiping blood from his face during a police lathicharge ordered by the then UP govt against Ram temple activists should remain etched in the memory of the youth for 100 years."Ashok ji believed that one should remain committed to Hindutva because the welfare of the entire universe is possible only on the basis of the ideals of Hindutva," Shah said.Born into a well-off family, Singhal joined RSS and later became the fiery face of the temple movement as a VHP leader. He is credited with expanding the defining Hindutva movement by bringing deprived sections of society, especially sections of Dalits and tribals, under its fold.When a nation and society do not remember their heroes and fail to take their lives and teachings to the youth, an ideological vacuum emerges, Shah said, calling for promotion of Singhal's life story.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: European buildings are collecting human urine and turning it into fertiliser, with systems processing 3 million litres a year
articles.summary: A toilet in an office or apartment building usually has a simple purpose: waste goes in, water carries it away and the sewage system takes over.
articles.body: A toilet in an office or apartment building usually has a simple purpose: waste goes in, water carries it away and the sewage system takes over. In parts of Europe, that routine is being redesigned. Special toilets can separate urine before it is diluted with flushing water, allowing the liquid to be collected inside the building and treated as a source of plant nutrients. The approach is now operating in commercial and residential properties, including the European Space Agency's headquarters in Paris and a major private bank in Geneva. Across several installations, around 3 million litres of urine are being recycled each year. The resulting product can be used as fertiliser, while recovered water can return to the building's flushing system.The Swiss technology separating urine from ordinary wastewaterThe system depends on catching urine before it becomes part of a much larger stream of wastewater. Specially designed toilets and urinals direct the liquid through separate pipes without adding large amounts of flush water. That makes a difference because ordinary sewage contains a mixture of water, urine, faeces and other household waste. Separating the urine while it is still concentrated means the nutrients can be recovered without first treating an enormous volume of diluted wastewater.VunaNexus, a Swiss company developing this approach, has installed its technology in several large buildings. The treatment equipment can sit in the basement, turning what normally disappears into the sewer into a separate material that can be processed and reused.From building toilets to a bottle of fertiliserOnce collected, the urine goes through several treatment stages. The process removes unwanted substances, including micropollutants such as traces of medicines, while concentrating nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus.The liquid is then pasteurised at about 90C to deal with pathogens. Water is separated during the process and can be recovered for reuse, including for flushing toilets. What remains becomes Aurin, a liquid fertiliser produced from human urine. The product is not simply untreated urine being poured onto farmland. VunaNexus says its fertiliser has been approved for use on plants by authorities in Switzerland and France, and it is being sold for agricultural, gardening and household applications.How urine recycling is moving into major buildings across EuropeOne of the better-known installations is at the European Space Agency's headquarters in Paris. Instead of sending urine straight into the conventional sewage network, the building's toilets direct it towards a treatment unit.The technology is also operating in Switzerland, including at one of the country's largest private banks in Geneva. Taken together with other commercial and residential installations, VunaNexus says its systems are now recycling roughly 3 million litres of urine each year, as reported by European Space Agency (ESA). A larger development is also under way in Paris. The technology is being incorporated into a newly developed eco-neighbourhood, which is expected to become the company's biggest urine-recycling project in Europe.The nutrients are valuable because plants need themHuman urine contains nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, the same broad group of nutrients associated with conventional plant fertilisers. The attraction is less about the urine itself than about recovering these nutrients before they are lost into the wastewater stream.There is already a wider European push to make use of this resource. In France, Toopi Organics has been collecting urine from places including motorway service areas, public venues and music festivals and processing it into microbial plant biostimulants. The company has said it wants to distribute more than 5 million litres of urine-based biostimulants across Europe by 2029. Projects in the Netherlands and Sweden have also explored urine collection for agricultural use. At the Dutch Zwarte Cross festival, for example, around 60,000 litres of urine were collected and converted into ammonium sulphate fertiliser.How Wales is testing recycled urine fertiliser for new forestsThe idea is moving beyond food crops. In Wales, a three-year Forestry Commission-backed project is testing urine-derived fertiliser on young native trees. Bristol-based NPK Recovery has been collecting urine from portable toilets at events including the London Marathon and Boomtown Festival. Its treatment process uses nutrients recovered from the liquid to produce fertiliser that has already been tested on grass and crops.The new trial involves Stump up for Trees and a nursery near Abergavenny. The partners plan to use the fertiliser while growing 4,500 native British trees, including beech and Scots pine, before planting them in Bannau Brycheiniog National Park. The project has received a £435,627 Forestry Commission grant.It is a different setting from a bank or office, but the basic principle is similar: keep urine separate, recover its nutrients and put them back into a useful biological cycle.How festivals are turning toilets into nutrient recovery systemsLarge public events produce an unusual opportunity for urine recovery because thousands of people use temporary toilets within a concentrated area. Instead of transporting the waste as conventional sewage, collection systems can capture some of the nutrients where they are produced.NPK Recovery has used events such as the London Marathon and Boomtown to build experience with collection and processing. Other European companies are pursuing similar arrangements with festivals, public toilets, motorway facilities and other high-use sites.The approach also changes the role of the toilet itself. Rather than being only the first stage in a waste-disposal chain, it becomes part of a system designed to recover materials.Why scaling urine recycling remains difficultThere are limits to how far the technology can go. Recovering nitrogen from urine remains more expensive than producing synthetic fertiliser in some small-scale systems, particularly when the cost of collection and treatment is included. VunaNexus has said that scaling up the technology and recognising the wastewater-treatment benefits will be important to its economics.The collection problem is also real. A treatment plant needs a reliable supply of separated urine, while buildings need specially designed plumbing and toilets. Transporting large quantities over long distances can undermine some of the benefits.That helps explain why buildings, festivals and other places where urine can be separated at source are becoming important test sites.A different route for nutrients that normally disappearVunaNexus estimates that recycling urine across Europe could provide around 30% of the region's nitrogen requirement. That is a company estimate rather than an indication that urine recycling could replace the fertiliser industry, but it illustrates the scale of the nutrient stream being considered. The technology is therefore being tested as part of a wider shift in how cities handle waste and resources. Urine is mostly water, but the small fraction containing nutrients can be isolated before it becomes mixed with everything else.At the European Space Agency's headquarters, in a Geneva bank and in new developments in Paris, that process is already happening inside buildings. In Wales, a related idea is being taken into a tree nursery. And at festivals, the same material is being collected from temporary toilets before it is lost to the conventional sewage system.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: LPU protests: Over 2,000 police deployed after stone-pelting, vehicles set ablaze
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Punjab Police deployed more than 2,000 personnel at Lovely Professional University (LPU) after student protests over an alleged rape case
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Punjab Police deployed more than 2,000 personnel at Lovely Professional University (LPU) after student protests over an alleged rape case turned violent on Sunday, with senior officers saying the situation had been brought under control.ADGP M F Farooqui told news agency ANI, that the force would remain deployed on campus through the night to maintain security.“We will ensure security on the campus throughout the night... A force of over 2,000 personnel is currently deployed here. Law and order has been fully maintained and restored... The process is ongoing, and we are working to keep the situation under control,” Farooqui told ANI.He appealed to families not to panic, saying, “To the families whose daughters are staying in the hostel here: please do not worry; everyone is safe... The atmosphere here is completely calm, and the university students are also cooperating with us in restoring peace...”Fresh violence erupted on Sunday evening after the protesting students pelted stones at police personnel and attacked their vehicles, leaving several cops injured, officials said.The protests began after claims circulated on social media about the alleged rape of a university student on the LPU campus. Students later blocked National Highway 44 outside the university from around 8 am, according to officials.Police said the situation escalated when protesters allegedly pelted stones at personnel and attacked police vehicles. Officers used a lathi charge as they attempted to clear the highway, after which protesters moved towards the campus.Two police vehicles were set on fire, while several police personnel were injured.Jalandhar Police Commissioner Satinder Singh said reports of disturbances inside hostels were rumours and that checks had found no such incidents.“First of all, reports of disturbances in the hostels were merely rumours. All hostels have been checked, and there are no issues. Traffic has resumed, and the situation is normal,” Singh said.He added, “Other matters will be resolved through discussions with the students... Overall, the atmosphere is fine, and any minor issues will be addressed... Please inform the families that all students are safe and there is no cause for concern.”DIG (Jalandhar Range) Naveen Singla also said, “The situation has been brought under control. Traffic movement on NH-44 will be restored soon.”Meanwhile, LPU postponed its mid-term examinations until further notice and suspended regular classes for 10 days from September 28. The university urged students to remain calm, follow official instructions and stay connected for further updates.Police said the deployment would continue overnight as authorities work to maintain order on campus and assess the situation.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
